---
title: "Interpreting a linear regression"
---

## Packages

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
```

## Back to Sacramento

On Monday we fit `price ~ sqft` on the Sacramento house sales.
Let's add `type`, a categorical variable,
so we can see how to read both kinds of variables.

```{r}
Sacramento |>
  count(type)
```

## Dummy variables

- A regression needs numbers,
  so R turns a categorical variable (a factor)
  into **dummy variables**, also called indicator variables
- Each dummy variable is a 0/1 column for one level,
  and there's one for every level except the first
- The level without a column is the **reference level**,
  and every other level gets compared with it

## Two names for the same idea

- Statistics calls this **dummy variable encoding**
- Computer science and machine learning call it **one-hot encoding**
- Both turn each level of a categorical variable into a 0/1 column
- One-hot encoding usually keeps a column for every level,
  while a regression with an intercept drops one,
  the reference level (R does this for us)

## `type` as dummy variables

`type` has 3 levels, so it becomes 2 dummy variables,
with `Condo` as the reference:

| `type` | `typeMulti_Family` | `typeResidential` |
|---|:-:|:-:|
| `Condo` | 0 | 0 |
| `Multi_Family` | 1 | 0 |
| `Residential` | 0 | 1 |

## Fit the model

```{r}
house_fit <- linear_reg() |>
  fit(price ~ sqft + type, data = Sacramento)

house_tidy <- tidy(house_fit, conf.int = TRUE)
house_tidy
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# pull one number out of the tidy table, for the sentences on the next slides
get_value <- function(term, column = "estimate") {
  house_tidy[[column]][house_tidy$term == term]
}
usd <- scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)
```

- One row for `sqft`
- One row for each dummy variable,
  and no row for `Condo`, the reference level

## Interpreting a continuous variable

> For every 1 [unit] increase in [variable],
> we expect [outcome] to increase (or decrease) by [estimate] [units],
> all else remaining the same.

For `sqft`:

> For every 1 square foot increase in size,
> we expect the sale price to increase by `r usd(get_value("sqft"))`,
> all else remaining the same
> (95% CI: `r usd(get_value("sqft", "conf.low"))` to `r usd(get_value("sqft", "conf.high"))`).

- "All else remaining the same" means the other variables in the model,
  so here, a house of the same `type`

## Interpreting a categorical variable

> We expect [outcome] for [level] to be [estimate] [units] higher (or lower)
> than for [reference level],
> all else remaining the same.

For `typeMulti_Family`:

> We expect multi-family homes to sell for
> `r usd(abs(get_value("typeMulti_Family")))` less than condos,
> all else remaining the same
> (95% CI: `r usd(abs(get_value("typeMulti_Family", "conf.high")))`
> to `r usd(abs(get_value("typeMulti_Family", "conf.low")))` less).

- Here "all else" is the size:
  a multi-family home and a condo with the same square footage
- The comparison is always with the reference level, `Condo`

## When the interval includes 0

For `typeResidential`:

> We expect residential homes to sell for
> `r usd(get_value("typeResidential"))` more than condos,
> all else remaining the same
> (95% CI: `r usd(get_value("typeResidential", "conf.low"))` to `r usd(get_value("typeResidential", "conf.high"))`).

- The interval includes 0,
  so the data don't show a clear difference
  between residential homes and condos of the same size
- We still report the estimate and its interval,
  and say that it's unclear

## The intercept

- The intercept is the expected outcome
  when every continuous variable is 0
  and every categorical variable is at its reference level
- Here that's a condo with 0 square feet,
  which doesn't exist,
  so we don't interpret it

## The same model in base R

Base R's `lm()` fits the same model with less code:

```{r}
lm(price ~ sqft + type, data = Sacramento) |>
  tidy(conf.int = TRUE)
```

- The same estimates and intervals as `linear_reg()`
- We use tidymodels because every kind of model goes through the same steps

- `Sacramento`: from modeldata, loaded with tidymodels
- Interpreting coefficients follows chapter 8 of
